Then $\mathbb{D}''$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ and by the construction it has the required properties (see also Lemma \ref{transport} and the proof of Proposition \ref{strictext}).
nodes.statement_short: Transport the induced $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\fr}$-derivation on $C$ along the isomorphism $\fr_C^{-1}:C\cong C^{1/p}$.

nodes.name: Claim 2
nodes.statement: There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types: $$\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum _{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{t,i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})};$$ where $b\in B$, $s<\kappa$, $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, $j\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}$ and $\alpha_{i,l},\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}\in K$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathfrak{m}$ has generators of two shapes: pure $p$-th power relations and triangular linear relations in the earlier variables.
conclusions: There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types:

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators. In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$. Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build the generating set in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot\kappa$ steps, splitting at each step according to whether the new value already lies in the field generated so far.

nodes.name: Set up the step-by-step construction
nodes.statement: We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: The generators are produced in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot\kappa$ steps.

nodes.name: Step (0,1)
nodes.statement: In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators.
nodes.statement_short: Add $X^p-b_0$ to the empty generating set.

nodes.name: Step (0,2): two cases
nodes.statement: In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators.
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$ lies in $K^p(b_0)$.

nodes.name: Step (0,3) and iteration
nodes.statement: In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat with the field enlarged by the previous value.

nodes.name: Conclude for every $b_s$
nodes.statement: Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$.
nodes.statement_short: After $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps the generators for $b_0$ are complete; iterate over $B$.

nodes.name: The idea behind the construction, and differential perfectness
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof above may seem to be technical, but the idea is very simple. For $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, the value $D_{\mathbf{j}}(a^{1/p})$ is determined by Claim 1. For $i\leqslant e$, we set $D_{(p^{m-1})_i}(a^{1/p})$ as a new formal variable. The values of the remaining operators on $a^{1/p}$ are determined by the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity rule. \item \item The above proof may be also used to show that a $\mathfrak{g}$-field is strict if and only if it is \emph{differentially perfect}, i.e. each of its differential extension is separable. This generalizes a result of Kolchin (see Chapter II, Section 3., Proposition 5.(a) in \cite{kol1}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Only the top-order values $D_{(p^{m-1})_i}(a^{1/p})$ are free; the argument also shows strict = differentially perfect.

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on a tensor product
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-rings. Then there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms.
conclusions: there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms

nodes.name: Proof of the tensor product lemma
nodes.statement: It is convenient to show a more general result. Assume that $V,W$ are schemes over $k$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ and $\mathbb{D}_W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $V$ and $W$ respectively. As in the case of the usual group actions, we get a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ such that the projections $V\times W\to V,W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant. By considering the affine schemes and dualizing, we get what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the scheme-level statement (a unique action on $V\times W$ with invariant projections) and dualize.

nodes.name: Pass to a more general scheme statement
nodes.statement: It is convenient to show a more general result. Assume that $V,W$ are schemes over $k$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ and $\mathbb{D}_W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $V$ and $W$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: It is convenient to work with $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on schemes $V,W$.

nodes.name: Product action
nodes.statement: As in the case of the usual group actions, we get a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ such that the projections $V\times W\to V,W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: There is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ with $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant projections.

nodes.name: Dualize
nodes.statement: By considering the affine schemes and dualizing, we get what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Dualizing the affine case gives the ring statement.

nodes.name: Amalgamation over a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_1,\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_2$ be $\mathfrak{g}$-field extensions and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is strict. Then $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field.
conclusions: $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field

nodes.name: Proof of the amalgamation property over strict fields
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, we can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are separably closed (since separable algebraic extensions are \'{e}tale). Then $K^{\sep}$ is a subfield of $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Remark \ref{defgen}(5), it is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} (using Corollary \ref{dimconstants}), the $\mathfrak{g}$-field structure on $K^{\sep}$ is strict. Therefore we can assume that $K$ is separably closed as well. \\ The proof will be finished exactly as in \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2}. We can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are subfields of a big field $\Omega$ and that they are algebraically disjoint over $K$. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}, the extension $K\subseteq L_1$ is separable. Since $K$ is separably closed, this extension is regular (see \cite[p. 367]{lang2002algebra}). By \cite[Thm. VIII 4.12]{lang2002algebra}, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$, thus $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain. By Lemma \ref{forap}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ extending those on $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext} again, we get the required $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the field of fractions of $L_1\otimes_KL_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to separably closed $K,L_1,L_2$, make $L_1,L_2$ algebraically disjoint so $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain, then transport the $\mathfrak{g}$-structure to its fraction field.

nodes.name: Reduce to separably closed $L_1,L_2$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, we can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are separably closed (since separable algebraic extensions are \'{e}tale).
nodes.statement_short: Separable algebraic extensions are étale, so the derivations extend.

nodes.name: Reduce to separably closed $K$
nodes.statement: Then $K^{\sep}$ is a subfield of $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Remark \ref{defgen}(5), it is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} (using Corollary \ref{dimconstants}), the $\mathfrak{g}$-field structure on $K^{\sep}$ is strict. Therefore we can assume that $K$ is separably closed as well. \\
nodes.statement_short: $K^{\sep}$ is a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield, so we may assume $K$ separably closed.

nodes.name: Linear disjointness gives a domain
nodes.statement: The proof will be finished exactly as in \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2}. We can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are subfields of a big field $\Omega$ and that they are algebraically disjoint over $K$. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}, the extension $K\subseteq L_1$ is separable. Since $K$ is separably closed, this extension is regular (see \cite[p. 367]{lang2002algebra}). By \cite[Thm. VIII 4.12]{lang2002algebra}, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$, thus $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity of $K\subseteq L_1$ makes $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ a domain.

nodes.name: Transport to the fraction field
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{forap}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ extending those on $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext} again, we get the required $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the field of fractions of $L_1\otimes_KL_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Put the $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the tensor product and extend it étale-ly to its fraction field.

nodes.name: Standing assumption $\mathfrak{g}=W[m]$
nodes.statement: In this subsection, we assume that $\mathfrak{g}$ is of the form $W[m]$ for a formal group law $W$ (see Remark \ref{intgs}).

nodes.name: $p$-th root function $\lambda$
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p$ and $\lambda$ be the following \emph{$p$-th root function}: $$\lambda:K\to K,\ \ \ \lambda(x)= \begin{cases} x^{1/p}\text{ for }x\in K^p, \\ 0\ \ \ \ \text{ for }x\notin K^p. \end{cases}$$

nodes.name: The languages $L^{\lambda}$, $L_{e,m}$, $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$
nodes.statement: We introduce several languages. \begin{itemize} \item Let $L^{\lambda}$ be the language of rings expanded by a unary function symbol $\lambda$. \item Let $L_{e,m}$ be the language of $k$-algebras (so there are constants in the language for the elements of $k$) with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations. \item Let $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}=L^{\lambda}\cup L_{e,m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rings with a unary $\lambda$, $k$-algebras with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations, and their union.

nodes.name: Basic properties of $L^{\lambda}$-extensions
nodes.statement: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure and we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$. \item If $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L_{e,m}$-extension and $\mathbf{K}$ is strict, then $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension. \item Suppose $R$ is a subring of a field $L$, $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ and $R\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. Then $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $L^{\lambda}$-extensions are exactly those with $L^p\cap K=K^p$; strictness upgrades $L_{e,m}$-extensions, and the property passes to fraction fields.
assumptions: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure
conclusions: A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$.
If $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L_{e,m}$-extension and $\mathbf{K}$ is strict, then $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension.
Suppose $R$ is a subring of a field $L$, $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ and $R\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. Then $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension.

nodes.name: Proof of the lemma on $L^{\lambda}$-extensions
nodes.statement: The item $(1)$ is clear and $(2)$ follows from Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(2). The last item follows by an easy computation.
nodes.statement_short: (1) is immediate, (2) is separability from the linear-disjointness lemma, and (3) is a direct computation.

nodes.name: Items (1) and (2)
nodes.statement: The item $(1)$ is clear and $(2)$ follows from Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(2).
nodes.statement_short: Item (1) is clear; item (2) is separability.

nodes.name: Item (3)
nodes.statement: The last item follows by an easy computation.
nodes.statement_short: Item (3) by computation.

nodes.name: Elementary extensions of separably closed fields are the étale ones
nodes.statement: Let us assume that $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree. Then the following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. \item The $K$-algebra $L$ is \'{e}tale. \item The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings). \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary. \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L_{e,m}$-elementary. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Same absolute $p$-basis, étale, elementary in rings, $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and $L_{e,m}$-elementary are all equivalent.
assumptions: Let us assume that $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree.
conclusions: The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis.
The $K$-algebra $L$ is \'{e}tale.
The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings).
The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary.
The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L_{e,m}$-elementary.

nodes.name: Proof of the elementary/étale equivalence
nodes.statement: By the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Del1} and by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1}, the extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary if and only if $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. By \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}, it happens if and only if this extension is \'{e}tale, so we get the equivalence of $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$. \\ Since both the $\lambda$-function and the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation are defined (over the field of the $p^m$-th powers) using the field operations and the elements of a $p$-basis, we get the equivalence of $(3)$ with $(4)$ and $(5)$.
nodes.statement_short: Delon's characterization gives (1)–(3); the $\lambda$-function and the derivation are $p$-basis definable, giving (4) and (5).

nodes.name: Equivalence of (1), (2) and (3)
nodes.statement: By the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Del1} and by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1}, the extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary if and only if $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. By \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}, it happens if and only if this extension is \'{e}tale, so we get the equivalence of $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$. \\
nodes.statement_short: Combine \cite{Del1} with \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}.

nodes.name: Equivalence with (4) and (5)
nodes.statement: Since both the $\lambda$-function and the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation are defined (over the field of the $p^m$-th powers) using the field operations and the elements of a $p$-basis, we get the equivalence of $(3)$ with $(4)$ and $(5)$.
nodes.statement_short: Both extra structures are defined from the field operations and a $p$-basis.

nodes.name: The theories $\gdf$, $\gdf_{\lambda}$, $\gdcf$, $\gdcf_{\lambda}$
nodes.statement:
We introduce now several theories.  egin{itemize} \item Let $\gdf$ be the theory of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields in the language $L_{e,m}$. \item Let $\gdf_{\lambda}$ be the theory of strict $\mathfrak{g}$-fields in the language $L_{e,m}^{\lambda}$ i.e. $\gdf_{\lambda}$ contains the natural interpretation of $\lambda$ and the following extra axiom: $$ orall x \Big((x
eq 0\ \wedge \ \lambda(x)=0)\ ightarrow\ (D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)}(x)
eq 0\ \vee\ \ldots \vee D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}(x)
eq 0)\Big).$$ \item Let $\gdcf$ be the theory $\gdf$ with the extra axioms for strict $\mathfrak{g}$-fields, and for separably closed fields of imperfectness degree $e$. \item Similarly for $\gdcf_{\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathfrak{g}$-fields, strict $\mathfrak{g}$-fields with $\lambda$, and their separably-closed-of-imperfectness-degree-$e$ enrichments.

nodes.name: Consistency of $\gdcf$ and $\gdcf_{\lambda}$
nodes.statement: The theories $\gdcf$ and $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ are consistent.
conclusions: The theories $\gdcf$ and $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ are consistent.

nodes.name: Proof of consistency
nodes.statement: We take the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^F$ on the field $K$ from Example \ref{canex}. By Proposition \ref{canstrict}, $\mathbf{K}$ is strict and clearly the imperfection degree of $K$ is $e$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ extends to the separable closure of $K$ (a separable algebraic extension is \'{e}tale, see \cite[Thm. 26.7]{mat}). By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(3), this extension is still strict. Since it is \'{e}tale, the degree of imperfection does not change.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a model: the canonical $F$-derivation on $k((\mathbf{X}))$, extended to the separable closure.

nodes.name: Take the canonical $F$-derivation
nodes.statement: We take the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^F$ on the field $K$ from Example \ref{canex}. By Proposition \ref{canstrict}, $\mathbf{K}$ is strict and clearly the imperfection degree of $K$ is $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Start from $\mathbb{D}^F$ on $K$ from the canonical example; it is strict of imperfection degree $e$.

nodes.name: Extend to the separable closure
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ extends to the separable closure of $K$ (a separable algebraic extension is \'{e}tale, see \cite[Thm. 26.7]{mat}).
nodes.statement_short: Separable algebraic extensions are étale, so the derivation extends.

nodes.name: Strictness and degree survive
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(3), this extension is still strict. Since it is \'{e}tale, the degree of imperfection does not change.
nodes.statement_short: Strictness and the imperfection degree are preserved along étale extensions.

nodes.name: Embedding into an elementary extension (the QE criterion input)
nodes.statement: Let us take $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{F}$ being a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. Then there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$ sharing a substructure with a model $\mathbf{L}$ of $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ embeds over it into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$.
assumptions: Let us take $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{F}$ being a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field
assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$
conclusions: there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$

nodes.name: Proof of the elementary amalgamation proposition
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(1), Proposition \ref{etalegext} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(3), we can assume that $K$ is a field. By Lemma \ref{lamb}(1), we have $K^p=L^p\cap K$. Since $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and hence $\mathbf{K}$ is strict as well. By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(2), we can $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable, by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} there is an elementary extension in the language of fields $L\preccurlyeq L'$ and a field embedding $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$. The situation is described in the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{ & & L'\\ & \mathbf{F}'\ar[ru]^{\Upsilon} & \\ \mathbf{F}\ar[ru]^{} & & \mathbf{L}\ar[lu]^{} \ar[uu]^{\preccurlyeq}\\ & \mathbf{K}\ar[ru]^{}\ar[lu]^{}. & } \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale. The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$ is strict, so by Corollary \ref{dimconstants}, we have $[F':(F')^p]\leqslant p^e$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable and $[L:L^p]=p^e$, by the equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is \'{e}tale. Then the extension $F'\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale as well. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $L'$ extending the one on $F'$ (hence also extending the one on $L$). By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $\mathbf{L}\subseteq \mathbf{L}'$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathbf{F}'$, embed $F'$ into an elementary extension $L'$, and check every extension in sight is étale so the derivation extends.

nodes.name: Reduce to $K$ a strict field
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(1), Proposition \ref{etalegext} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(3), we can assume that $K$ is a field. By Lemma \ref{lamb}(1), we have $K^p=L^p\cap K$. Since $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and hence $\mathbf{K}$ is strict as well.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the fraction field and note $\mathbf{K}$ inherits strictness from $\mathbf{L}$.

nodes.name: Amalgamate into $\mathbf{F}'$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(2), we can $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamation over the strict $\mathbf{K}$ produces a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$.

nodes.name: Embed $F'$ into an elementary extension $L'$
nodes.statement: Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable, by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} there is an elementary extension in the language of fields $L\preccurlyeq L'$ and a field embedding $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$. The situation is described in the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{ & & L'\\ & \mathbf{F}'\ar[ru]^{\Upsilon} & \\ \mathbf{F}\ar[ru]^{} & & \mathbf{L}\ar[lu]^{} \ar[uu]^{\preccurlyeq}\\ & \mathbf{K}\ar[ru]^{}\ar[lu]^{}. & } \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Separability plus \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} gives $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$.

nodes.name: All the extensions are étale
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale. The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$ is strict, so by Corollary \ref{dimconstants}, we have $[F':(F')^p]\leqslant p^e$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable and $[L:L^p]=p^e$, by the equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is \'{e}tale. Then the extension $F'\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale as well.
nodes.statement_short: Degree bounds force $L\subseteq F'$ and then $F'\subseteq L'$ to be étale.

nodes.name: Extend the derivation to $L'$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $L'$ extending the one on $F'$ (hence also extending the one on $L$). By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $\mathbf{L}\subseteq \mathbf{L}'$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Extend along the étale map and conclude $\mathbf{L}\subseteq\mathbf{L}'$ is elementary.

nodes.name: $\gdcf$ is the model companion of $\gdf$
nodes.statement: We have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$. \item Each model of $\gdf$ embeds into a model of $\gdcf$. \item The theory $\gdcf$ is a model companion of the theory $\gdf$. \item The theory $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\gdf_{\lambda}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ eliminates quantifiers and is the model completion of $\gdf_{\lambda}$; $\gdcf$ is the model companion of $\gdf$.
conclusions: The theory $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$.
Each model of $\gdf$ embeds into a model of $\gdcf$.
The theory $\gdcf$ is a model companion of the theory $\gdf$.
The theory $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\gdf_{\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the model companion theorem
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we use the criterion from \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} (and Proposition \ref{elemamal}) exactly as in \cite[3.1]{Zieg2}. \\ For $(2)$, let us take any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$. By Proposition \ref{gstrictexist}, we may assume that $\mathbf{F}$ is strict. By Lemma \ref{consistent}, there is $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$. Clearly, $k$ with the trivial $\mathfrak{g}$-structure is a common $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. By Proposition \ref{elemamal}, $\mathbf{F}$ embeds into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$, which is clearly a model of $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ as well. \\ By $(1)$, $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ is model complete, so using Lemma \ref{lamb}(2) and Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, we get that $\gdcf$ is model complete as well. By $(2)$, $\gdcf$ is a model companion of the theory $\gdf$, so we get $(3)$. \\ By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and the item $(1)$, we get $(4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Sacks' QE criterion to the elementary amalgamation proposition, then derive embedding, model completeness and model completion.

nodes.name: Part (1): quantifier elimination
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we use the criterion from \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} (and Proposition \ref{elemamal}) exactly as in \cite[3.1]{Zieg2}. \\
nodes.statement_short: Use the criterion \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} together with the elementary amalgamation proposition.

nodes.name: Part (2): every model embeds
nodes.statement: For $(2)$, let us take any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$. By Proposition \ref{gstrictexist}, we may assume that $\mathbf{F}$ is strict. By Lemma \ref{consistent}, there is $\mathbf{L}\models \gdcf_{\lambda}$. Clearly, $k$ with the trivial $\mathfrak{g}$-structure is a common $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. By Proposition \ref{elemamal}, $\mathbf{F}$ embeds into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$, which is clearly a model of $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ as well. \\
nodes.statement_short: Make $\mathbf{F}$ strict, take a model of $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ and embed over the common substructure $k$.

nodes.name: Part (3): model companion
nodes.statement: By $(1)$, $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ is model complete, so using Lemma \ref{lamb}(2) and Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, we get that $\gdcf$ is model complete as well. By $(2)$, $\gdcf$ is a model companion of the theory $\gdf$, so we get $(3)$. \\
nodes.statement_short: Transfer model completeness from $\gdcf_{\lambda}$ to $\gdcf$.

nodes.name: Part (4): model completion
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and the item $(1)$, we get $(4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Model completion from AP and QE.

nodes.name: Failures for $\gdf$ and relations to other theories
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\gdf$ does not have the amalgamation property. The theory $\gdcf$ does not have quantifier elimination and the theory $\gdcf$ is not a model completion of the theory $\gdf$. \item We have (after taking $k=\Ff_p$) $$\ga^e[m]-\dcf =\sch_{p,e,m},$$ where $\sch_{p,e,m}$ is the theory considered in \cite{K3}. \item If we take the algebraic group $U$ from Example \ref{gitex}(2), then a $U(1)$-field is the same as a field with two derivations $\partial_1,\partial_2$ such that $\partial_1^{(p)}=\partial_2$ and $\partial_2^{(p)}=0$. Hence $U(1)-\dcf$ corresponds to Wood's theory $2-\dcf$, see \cite{Wo2}. It should be possible to find algebraic groups governing the iterative rules for Wood's theories $m-\dcf$ for an arbitrary $m$. \item After dropping the iterativity assumptions rather strange things happen. In the case of characteristic zero, model companions exist and are analyzed in \cite{MS2}. In the case of positive characteristic, it is shown in \cite[Prop 7.2]{MS2} that (in our terminology) the theory of fields with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations has a model companion if and only if $m=1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\gdf$ lacks amalgamation and $\gdcf$ lacks QE; $\ga^e[m]-\dcf$ recovers $\sch_{p,e,m}$ and $U(1)-\dcf$ recovers Wood's $2-\dcf$.

nodes.name: The language $L_e$ and the theories $\fdf$, $\fdcf$
nodes.statement: Let $L_e$ be the language of $k$-algebras with $e$-dimensional HS-derivations. The main model-theoretic advantage of HS-derivations (over truncated HS-derivations) is that we do not need to consider the extra operator $\lambda$ to get quantifier elimination results. \\ We define two $L_e$-theories. \begin{itemize} \item Let $\fdf$ be the theory of $F$-fields. \item Let $\fdcf$ be the theory $\fdf$ with the extra axioms for strict $F$-fields, and for separably closed fields of imperfection degree $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Full (non-truncated) HS-derivations need no $\lambda$; $\fdcf$ adds strictness and separable closedness of imperfection degree $e$ to $\fdf$.

nodes.name: Transport of a derivation along a ring isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $f\in \aut(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$. For any $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$, we define: $$\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:S\to S[\mathbf{v}_m],\ \ \ \mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:=\varphi[\mathbf{v}_m]\circ \mathbb{D}\circ \varphi^{-1}.$$ Then $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation, where $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$ is the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugating $\mathbb{D}$ by an isomorphism $\varphi$ over $f\in\aut(k)$ gives a $\mathfrak{g}^f$-derivation.
assumptions: Let $f\in \aut(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$.
conclusions: $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation, where $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$ is the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by $f$

nodes.name: Smallest strict extension of an $F$-field
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}=(K,\mathbb{D})$ be an $F$-field. Then there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$.
conclusions: there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$

nodes.name: Proof of the smallest strict extension
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the field of constants of $\mathbf{K}$. It is enough to show that there is a unique $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $C^{1/p}$ extending $\mathbb{D}$. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(1), $C$ is an $F$-subfield of $K$. For $\mathbf{i}\in \Nn^e$ and $a\in C^{1/p}$, we have the only option (as in \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Zieg2}): $$D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a):=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}.$$ Clearly, each $D'_{\mathbf{i}}$ extends $D_{\mathbf{i}}$. We need to show that $\mathbb{D}'=(D'_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}\in \Nn^e}$ is an $F$-derivation. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2), the sequence of maps $$\mathbb{D}'':=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(b))_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}$$ is an $F[m-1]^{\fr}$-derivation on $C$. It is easy to see that $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ coincides with $\mathbb{D}''$ ``transported'' to $C^{1/p}$ using the ring isomorphism $\fr^{-1}_C:C\to C^{1/p}$. By Lemma \ref{transport}, $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ is an $F[m-1]$-derivation. Since it happens for all $m\in \Nn$, we get that $\mathbb{D}'$ is an $F$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: There is only one possible formula $D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a)=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}$ on $C^{1/p}$; transport shows it is an $F$-derivation.

nodes.name: Reduce to extending to $C^{1/p}$
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the field of constants of $\mathbf{K}$. It is enough to show that there is a unique $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $C^{1/p}$ extending $\mathbb{D}$. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(1), $C$ is an $F$-subfield of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to extend $\mathbb{D}$ uniquely to the $p$-th roots of the constants.

nodes.name: The only possible formula
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{i}\in \Nn^e$ and $a\in C^{1/p}$, we have the only option (as in \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Zieg2}): $$D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a):=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}.$$ Clearly, each $D'_{\mathbf{i}}$ extends $D_{\mathbf{i}}$. We need to show that $\mathbb{D}'=(D'_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}\in \Nn^e}$ is an $F$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: Define $D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a)=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}$, the sole option.

nodes.name: Identify $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ as a transport
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2), the sequence of maps $$\mathbb{D}'':=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(b))_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}$$ is an $F[m-1]^{\fr}$-derivation on $C$. It is easy to see that $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ coincides with $\mathbb{D}''$ ``transported'' to $C^{1/p}$ using the ring isomorphism $\fr^{-1}_C:C\to C^{1/p}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(D_{p\mathbf{i}})$ is an $F[m-1]^{\fr}$-derivation on $C$, transported along $\fr_C^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude it is an $F$-derivation
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{transport}, $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ is an $F[m-1]$-derivation. Since it happens for all $m\in \Nn$, we get that $\mathbb{D}'$ is an $F$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: Each truncation is an $F[m-1]$-derivation, so the limit is an $F$-derivation.

nodes.name: $F$-fields have the amalgamation property
nodes.statement: The class of $F$-fields has the amalgamation property.
conclusions: The class of $F$-fields has the amalgamation property.

nodes.name: $\fdcf$ is a model completion of $\fdf$
nodes.statement: The theory $\fdcf$ is a model completion of the theory $\fdf$ (so it eliminates quantifiers).
conclusions: The theory $\fdcf$ is a model completion of the theory $\fdf$ (so it eliminates quantifiers).

nodes.name: Why $\fdf$ behaves better than $\gdf$
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The extra property which makes the theory $\fdf$ nicer than the theory $\gdf$ is the existence of the \emph{smallest} strict extensions (Proposition \ref{strictext}). It gives the amalgamation property for \emph{all} (i.e. not necessarily strict) $F$-fields (Proposition \ref{apf}) and the quantifier elimination for $\fdcf$. \item In this context, quantifier elimination for $\fdcf$ implies elimination of imaginaries for $\fdcf$ exactly as in Section 4 of \cite{Zieg2}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Smallest strict extensions give amalgamation for all $F$-fields and hence QE, which in turn yields elimination of imaginaries.

nodes.name: $F-\dcf$ is the union of the chain $F[m]-\dcf$
nodes.statement: The theories $F[m]-\dcf$ form an increasing chain and we have $$F-\dcf = \bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}F[m]-\dcf.$$
conclusions: The theories $F[m]-\dcf$ form an increasing chain
$$F-\dcf = \bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}F[m]-\dcf.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the chain theorem
nodes.statement: It follows just by inspecting the axioms of the theories in question.
nodes.statement_short: Direct inspection of the axiom sets of the theories involved.

nodes.name: Can every model of $\scf_{p,e}$ be expanded to a model of $\fdcf$?
nodes.statement: In this subsection, we discuss the opposite problem: can any model of $\scf_{p,e}$ be expanded to a model of $\fdcf$? The same question can be asked for $\mathfrak{g}$ in place of $F$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: The languages $L^{\mathbf{b}}$, $L_e^{\mathbf{b}}$ and theories with a named $p$-basis
nodes.statement: By $L$, we denote the language of $k$-algebras, and by $\scf_{p,e}$, the theory of separably closed $k$-algebras with the degree of imperfection $e$ in the language $L$ (so our notation does not reflect the dependence on $k$, we hope it will not cause any confusion). Recall that $L_e$ denotes the language of $k$-algebras with $e$-dimensional HS-derivations. We introduce two new languages (obtained after adding $e$ extra constant symbols): $$L^{\mathbf{b}}:=L\cup\lbrace b_1,\ldots,b_e\rbrace,\qquad L_e^{\mathbf{b}}:=L_e\cup\lbrace b_1,\ldots,b_e\rbrace.$$ Let $\beta$ be a sentence in the language $L^{\mathbf{b}}$ saying that $b_1,\ldots,b_e$ form a $p$-basis. Now we add $\beta$ to the theory $\scf_{p,e}$ and to the theory $F-\dcf$ to obtain the theory $$\scf_{p,e}^{\mathbf{b}}:=\scf_{p,e}\;\cup\;\lbrace\beta\rbrace$$ in the language $L^{\mathbf{b}}$, and the theory $$F-\dcf^{\mathbf{b}}:=F-\dcf\;\cup\;\lbrace\beta\rbrace$$ in the language $L_e^{\mathbf{b}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Add $e$ constants $b_1,\ldots,b_e$ and the sentence $\beta$ saying they form a $p$-basis.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: A separating transcendence basis for $k(G)$
nodes.statement: There are $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in k(G)$ algebraically independent over $k$ such that the field extension $k(x_1,\ldots,x_e)\subseteq k(G)$ is finite and separable.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields
conclusions: There are $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in k(G)$ algebraically independent over $k$ such that the field extension $k(x_1,\ldots,x_e)\subseteq k(G)$ is finite and separable.

nodes.name: Proof of the separating basis lemma
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in \mathcal{O}_G$ be a sequence of local parameters (see Example \ref{cangex}). By Example \ref{cangex}, \cite[30.6(ii)]{mat} and Proposition on page 276 of \cite{mat0}, $\{x_1,\ldots,x_e\}$ is a $p$-basis of $\mathcal{O}_G$, so it is also a $p$-basis of $k(G)$. Hence the field extension $k(x_1,\ldots,x_e)\subseteq k(G)$ is finite and separable.
nodes.statement_short: Local parameters at the identity of $G$ form a $p$-basis of $\mathcal{O}_G$, hence of $k(G)$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Take local parameters
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in \mathcal{O}_G$ be a sequence of local parameters (see Example \ref{cangex}).
nodes.statement_short: Choose local parameters $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in\mathcal{O}_G$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: They form a $p$-basis of $k(G)$
nodes.statement: By Example \ref{cangex}, \cite[30.6(ii)]{mat} and Proposition on page 276 of \cite{mat0}, $\{x_1,\ldots,x_e\}$ is a $p$-basis of $\mathcal{O}_G$, so it is also a $p$-basis of $k(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity of $\mathcal{O}_G$ makes the parameters a $p$-basis.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Finite separability
nodes.statement: Hence the field extension $k(x_1,\ldots,x_e)\subseteq k(G)$ is finite and separable.
nodes.statement_short: A $p$-basis gives a finite separable extension $k(\mathbf{x})\subseteq k(G)$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Primitive element and defining polynomial $H$ for $k(G)$
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_e$ be as in Lemma \ref{finsep}. By Abel's theorem, there is $y\in k(G)$ such that $k(G)=k(x_1,\ldots,x_e,y)$. Let $H(X_1,\ldots,X_e,Y)\in k[X_1,\ldots,X_e,Y]$ be such that $H(x_1,\ldots,x_e,y)=0$ and the polynomial $H(x_1,\ldots,x_e,Y)$ is irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: $k(G)=k(\mathbf{x},y)$ for a primitive $y$ with irreducible minimal polynomial $H(\mathbf{x},Y)$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields
conclusions: there is $y\in k(G)$ such that $k(G)=k(x_1,\ldots,x_e,y)$

nodes.name: The languages $L^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ and the theories with the extra constant $c$
nodes.statement: We need to add one more constant to the languages we consider to obtain the following languages: $$L^{{\mathbf{b}},c}:=L\cup\lbrace b_1,\ldots,b_e,c\rbrace,\qquad L_e^{{\mathbf{b}},c}:=L_e\cup\lbrace b_1,\ldots,b_e,c\rbrace.$$ The meaning of this extra constant $c$ is that it generates the field $k(G)$ over $k$ extended by the chosen $p$-basis. Formally, we specify one more axiom $\gamma$ in the language $L^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ $$\gamma:=\ \ \beta \ \wedge \ (H(b_1,\ldots,b_e,c)=0).$$ We define the following theories. $$\scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}:=\scf_{p,e}\;\cup\;\lbrace \gamma\rbrace,\ \ F-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}:=F-\dcf\;\cup\;\lbrace \gamma\rbrace .$$
nodes.statement_short: One extra constant $c$ with axiom $\gamma=\beta\wedge H(b_1,\ldots,b_e,c)=0$ names a generator of $k(G)$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ is an extension by definitions of $\scf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}_{p,e}$
nodes.statement: The theory $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}_{p,e}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields
conclusions: The theory $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}_{p,e}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the bi-interpretability theorem
nodes.statement: Take $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in k(G)$ as in Lemma \ref{finsep}, denote $(x_1,\ldots,x_e)$ by $\mathbf{x}$ and let $y\in k(G)$ be separable algebraic over $k(\mathbf{x})$ such that $k(\mathbf{x},y)=k(G)$ (such $y$ exists by Lemma \ref{finsep} and Abel's theorem). Then for any $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in \Nn^e$, there are polynomials $F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}},H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}\in k[\mathbf{X},Y]$ such that for the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^{F}=(D_{\mathbf{j}}^F)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ on $k(G)$, we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}^F(\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{i}})=\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}\in k(G).$$ We describe now an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ coinciding with the theory $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. To ease the notation, we will also denote by $\mathbf{b}$ the tuple (of constant symbols or elements of a model) $(b_1,\ldots,b_e)$. Take $\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_e)\in\mathbb{N}^e$, for every $n\geqslant \max\lbrace j_1,\ldots,j_e\rbrace$ we add to the theory $\scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ the following defining axiom \begin{equation}\tag{$\clubsuit$} D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=y \leftrightarrow \left(\exists^{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\; \alpha_{\mathbf{i}}\right) \left(x=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\mathbf{b}^{\mathbf{i}} \;\wedge\; y=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)} \right). \end{equation} Take any $(K,\mathbf{b},c)\models \scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. It is not hard to verify that the defining axioms (\ref{scfD}) determine well-defined functions on $K$. The axioms $\beta,\gamma$ guarantee that $$k(\mathbf{b},c)\cong_k k(G)$$ and that $\mathbb{D}:=(D_{\mathbf{j}})_{\mathbf{j}\in \Nn^e}$ restricted to $k(\mathbf{b},c)$ corresponds to the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$. Because $\mathbf{b}$ is a $p$-basis of $K$, the extension $k(\mathbf{b})\subseteq K$ is \'{e}tale (see \cite[Theorem 26.8]{mat}). Hence the extension $k(\mathbf{b},c)\subseteq K$ is also \'{e}tale. Due to Proposition \ref{etalehs}, we can extend the canonical $G$-derivation from $k(G)$ to the field $K$. Let $\mathbb{D}'=\left(D'_{\mathbf{j}}\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ denote the $G$-derivation on $K$ extending the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$. Note that $D'_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)$ for every $x\in K$, hence $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$. Moreover the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$ is strict, so also $\mathbb{D}'|_{k(\mathbf{b},c)}$ is strict. Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} implies that $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$ is strict, so $(K,\mathbb{D},\mathbf{b},c)\models G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the operators $D_{\mathbf{j}}$ on the named $p$-basis by explicit rational formulas coming from the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$, then extend étale-ly to all of $K$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Choose the $p$-basis and primitive element
nodes.statement: Take $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in k(G)$ as in Lemma \ref{finsep}, denote $(x_1,\ldots,x_e)$ by $\mathbf{x}$ and let $y\in k(G)$ be separable algebraic over $k(\mathbf{x})$ such that $k(\mathbf{x},y)=k(G)$ (such $y$ exists by Lemma \ref{finsep} and Abel's theorem). Then for any $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in \Nn^e$, there are polynomials $F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}},H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}\in k[\mathbf{X},Y]$ such that for the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^{F}=(D_{\mathbf{j}}^F)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ on $k(G)$, we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}^F(\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{i}})=\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}\in k(G).$$
nodes.statement_short: Express $D_{\mathbf{j}}^F(\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{i}})$ as rational functions $F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}/H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}$ in $(\mathbf{x},y)$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Write the defining axioms
nodes.statement: We describe now an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ coinciding with the theory $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. To ease the notation, we will also denote by $\mathbf{b}$ the tuple (of constant symbols or elements of a model) $(b_1,\ldots,b_e)$. Take $\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_e)\in\mathbb{N}^e$, for every $n\geqslant \max\lbrace j_1,\ldots,j_e\rbrace$ we add to the theory $\scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ the following defining axiom \begin{equation}\tag{$\clubsuit$} D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=y \leftrightarrow \left(\exists^{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\; \alpha_{\mathbf{i}}\right) \left(x=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\mathbf{b}^{\mathbf{i}} \;\wedge\; y=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)} \right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define $D_{\mathbf{j}}$ on $p^n$-th power expansions in the named $p$-basis.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: The axioms recover $k(G)$
nodes.statement: Take any $(K,\mathbf{b},c)\models \scf_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. It is not hard to verify that the defining axioms (\ref{scfD}) determine well-defined functions on $K$. The axioms $\beta,\gamma$ guarantee that $$k(\mathbf{b},c)\cong_k k(G)$$ and that $\mathbb{D}:=(D_{\mathbf{j}})_{\mathbf{j}\in \Nn^e}$ restricted to $k(\mathbf{b},c)$ corresponds to the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\beta,\gamma$ force $k(\mathbf{b},c)\cong_k k(G)$ with the canonical $G$-derivation.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Extend the derivation to $K$
nodes.statement: Because $\mathbf{b}$ is a $p$-basis of $K$, the extension $k(\mathbf{b})\subseteq K$ is \'{e}tale (see \cite[Theorem 26.8]{mat}). Hence the extension $k(\mathbf{b},c)\subseteq K$ is also \'{e}tale. Due to Proposition \ref{etalehs}, we can extend the canonical $G$-derivation from $k(G)$ to the field $K$. Let $\mathbb{D}'=\left(D'_{\mathbf{j}}\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ denote the $G$-derivation on $K$ extending the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $k(\mathbf{b},c)\subseteq K$ is étale, so the canonical derivation extends uniquely.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Strictness and conclusion
nodes.statement: Note that $D'_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)$ for every $x\in K$, hence $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$. Moreover the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$ is strict, so also $\mathbb{D}'|_{k(\mathbf{b},c)}$ is strict. Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} implies that $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$ is strict, so $(K,\mathbb{D},\mathbf{b},c)\models G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$.
nodes.statement_short: The defined and extended derivations agree and are strict, giving a model of $G-\dcf^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: When the extra constant $c$ is unnecessary
nodes.statement: In many cases, the theory $G-\dcf^{\mathbf{b}}$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf^{{\mathbf{b}}}_{p,e}$, so in such cases the constant symbol $c$ is not necessary. For example, it is the case for $G$ being the group of Witt vectors, see \cite{Hoff2}.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Restricting the canonical derivation for an arbitrary formal group $F$
nodes.statement: It is unclear to us how to proceed in the case of an arbitrary formal group $F$. The crucial question is whether the canonical derivation on $k((\mathbf{X}))$ can be restricted to $k(\mathbf{X})$ or to $k(\mathbf{X})^{\sep}$. This question has been investigated in \cite{HK2} (it is related to Matsumura's \emph{integrability question}).
nodes.statement_short: Can the canonical derivation on $k((\mathbf{X}))$ be restricted to $k(\mathbf{X})$ or $k(\mathbf{X})^{\sep}$?
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Isomorphic formal group laws give extensions by definitions
nodes.statement: Assume that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are one-dimensional formal group laws over $k$ such that $F_1\cong F_2$. Then the theory $F_1-\dcf$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $F_2-\dcf$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields
assumptions: Assume that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are one-dimensional formal group laws over $k$ such that $F_1\cong F_2$.
conclusions: the theory $F_1-\dcf$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $F_2-\dcf$

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism-invariance lemma
nodes.statement: Let $f\in Xk\llbracket X\rrbracket$ be an isomorphism between $F_1$ and $F_2$. For any $F_1$-derivation $\mathbb{D}:K\to K\llbracket X\rrbracket$, the following composition \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{K \ar[r]^{\mathbb{D}} & K\llbracket X\rrbracket \ar[r]^{\ev_f} & K\llbracket X\rrbracket} \end{equation*} is an $F_2$-derivation. It is easy to see that for each positive integer $n$, there are $c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,n}\in k$ such that if $\mathbb{D}=(D_i)_{i\in \Nn}$ then the corresponding $F_2$-derivation $\ev_f\circ \mathbb{D}$ is of the form $$(\id,c_{1,1}D_1,c_{2,1}D_1+c_{2,2}D_2,\ldots),$$ hence the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Composing with $\ev_f$ turns an $F_1$-derivation into an $F_2$-derivation by a triangular change of the operators.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Take an isomorphism of formal group laws
nodes.statement: Let $f\in Xk\llbracket X\rrbracket$ be an isomorphism between $F_1$ and $F_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $f$ be an isomorphism between $F_1$ and $F_2$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Compose with $\ev_f$
nodes.statement: For any $F_1$-derivation $\mathbb{D}:K\to K\llbracket X\rrbracket$, the following composition \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{K \ar[r]^{\mathbb{D}} & K\llbracket X\rrbracket \ar[r]^{\ev_f} & K\llbracket X\rrbracket} \end{equation*} is an $F_2$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: $\ev_f\circ\mathbb{D}$ is an $F_2$-derivation.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Triangular change of operators
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that for each positive integer $n$, there are $c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,n}\in k$ such that if $\mathbb{D}=(D_i)_{i\in \Nn}$ then the corresponding $F_2$-derivation $\ev_f\circ \mathbb{D}$ is of the form $$(\id,c_{1,1}D_1,c_{2,1}D_1+c_{2,2}D_2,\ldots),$$ hence the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The new operators are $k$-combinations $c_{n,1}D_1+\ldots+c_{n,n}D_n$, so each is definable from the other.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: One-dimensional $F$ over an algebraically closed $k$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ is a one-dimensional formal group law over an algebraically closed field $k$ (in particular $e=1$). Then the theory $F-\dcf^{\mathbf{b}}$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf^{\mathbf{b}}_{p,1}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields
assumptions: Suppose that $F$ is a one-dimensional formal group law over an algebraically closed field $k$ (in particular $e=1$).
conclusions: the theory $F-\dcf^{\mathbf{b}}$ is an extension by definitions of the theory $\scf^{\mathbf{b}}_{p,1}$

nodes.name: Proof of the one-dimensional case
nodes.statement: By \cite[Thm. 4.3]{HK2}, there is a formal group law $\widetilde{F}$ over $k$ such that $F\cong \widetilde{F}$ and the canonical $\widetilde{F}$-derivation restricts to $k[X]$. By Lemma \ref{isodef}, we can assume that $F=\widetilde{F}$. We can repeat now the proof of Theorem \ref{biin} (and we do not need to worry about the extra constant $c$).
nodes.statement_short: Replace $F$ by an isomorphic $\widetilde{F}$ whose canonical derivation restricts to $k[X]$, then repeat the bi-interpretability proof.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Pick an integrable representative
nodes.statement: By \cite[Thm. 4.3]{HK2}, there is a formal group law $\widetilde{F}$ over $k$ such that $F\cong \widetilde{F}$ and the canonical $\widetilde{F}$-derivation restricts to $k[X]$.
nodes.statement_short: \cite[Thm. 4.3]{HK2} supplies $\widetilde{F}\cong F$ whose canonical derivation restricts to $k[X]$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Reduce to $F=\widetilde{F}$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{isodef}, we can assume that $F=\widetilde{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $F=\widetilde{F}$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Repeat the bi-interpretability argument
nodes.statement: We can repeat now the proof of Theorem \ref{biin} (and we do not need to worry about the extra constant $c$).
nodes.statement_short: The earlier proof applies with no need for the extra constant $c$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: Passing to the algebraic closure of the base field is harmless
nodes.statement: Passing from the base field $k$ to its algebraic closure expands the language with extra constants. But any existentially closed $F$-field is separably closed, so its field of absolute constants contains $k^{\alg}$. Hence such an expansion is not important for the theories we consider, since the models of $F-\dcf$ in the language with constants for elements of $k$ are the same as models of $F-\dcf$ in the language with constants for elements of $k^{\alg}$. Therefore, the assumption in Theorem \ref{onedimext} that $k$ is algebraically closed is harmless.
nodes.statement_short: Existentially closed $F$-fields already contain $k^{\alg}$ among their absolute constants, so naming those constants changes nothing.
nodes.section: 4.3 Bi-interpretability with a theory of separably closed fields

nodes.name: The functors $\mathcal{D}$, $\nabla$ and the map $\mathbb{D}_V$
nodes.statement:
We fix a field $K$ with a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation $\mathbb{D}$. Our first definitions do not use the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity condition.  egin{itemize} \item Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the functor from the category of $K$-algebras to the category of $K[\mathbf{v}_m]$-algebras defined in the following way: $$\mathcal{D}(R)=R\otimes_{K,\mathbb{D}}K[\mathbf{v}_m].$$ Since $\mathcal{D}$ commutes with localizations, it also defines a functor from $K$-schemes to $K[\mathbf{v}_m]$-schemes. \item The functor $\mathcal{D}$ considered as a functor from $K$-algebras to $K$-algebras has a left-adjoint functor $
abla$ which extends to $K$-schemes. A crucial natural bijection is the following one: $$(
abla V)(R)\longleftrightarrow V(\mathcal{D}(R)).$$ \item For any $K$-scheme $V$ we have a (non-algebraic!) map $$\mathbb{D}_{V}:V(K)	o V(\mathcal{D}(K))=
abla V(K)$$ induced by the $K$-algebra homomorphism $\mathbb{D}:K	o K[\mathbf{v}_m]=\mathcal{D}(K)$.

nodes.statement: Our notation here differs from the notation used in \cite{Bui2} and \cite{MS}, where the left-adjoint functor considered above is denoted $\tau$, and the notation $\nabla$ is used for $\mathbb{D}_{V}$.

nodes.statement:
The second set of definitions uses the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity condition.  egin{itemize} \item We have a natural transformation (of functors on the category of $K$-algebras) given by the Hopf algebra comultiplication (coming from $\mathfrak{g}$) $$\mu:\mathcal{D}	o \mathcal{D}\circ \mathcal{D}.$$ \item We define a natural transformation of functors on the category of $K$-schemes $$c:
abla	o

abla V(R) \ar[u]^{\cong} \ar[r]^{c_V} &

nodes.statement_short:
The Hopf comultiplication gives $\mu:\mathcal{D}	o\mathcal{D}\circ\mathcal{D}$, and dually $c:
abla	o

nodes.name: $K\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}$ and coordinates for $\nabla$, $\mathbb{D}_V$, $c_n$
nodes.statement:
For any positive integer $n$, our HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ naturally extends to the following HS-derivation $$\left(D_{\mathbf{j}}:K[X_1,\ldots,X_n]	o K[X_1^{(\mathbf{i})},\ldots,X_n^{(\mathbf{i})}\ |\ \mathbf{i}\in[p^m]^e\ ]ight)_{\mathbf{j}\in[p^m]^e},\ \ \mathbb{D}_{\mathbf{j}}(X)=X^{(\mathbf{j})},$$ where $X_k^{(\mathbf{0})}=X_k$ and for $\mathbf{j}
eq \mathbf{0}$, $X_k^{(\mathbf{j})}$ is a new variable. We will use the following notation $$K\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}:=K[X_1^{(\mathbf{i})},\ldots,X_n^{(\mathbf{i})}\ |\ \mathbf{i}\in[p^m]^e\ ].$$ If $R=K[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/I$, then $
abla(R)=K\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}/(\mathbb{D}(I))$. Hence, for an affine variety $V=\spec(R)$, the variety $
abla(V)$ is defined by the ideal $(\mathbb{D}(I))$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ is given in coordinates as the $n$-th Cartesian product of $\mathbb{D}$ (considered as a map from $K$ to $K^{p^{me}}$). \ Let $c_n$ denote $c_{\Aa^{np^{me}}}$. For every $(b_{\mathbf{i},1},\ldots,b_{\mathbf{i},n})_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}\in K^{np^{me}}$ we have $$c_n\left((b_{\mathbf{i},1},\ldots,b_{\mathbf{i},n})_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}ight)= \left(\sum\limits_{\mathbf{k}\in[p^m]^e}c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}b_{\mathbf{k},1},\ldots, \sum\limits_{\mathbf{k}\in[p^m]^e}c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}b_{\mathbf{k},n}ight)_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in [p^m]^e},$$ where $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}$ are the ``structural constants'' from Remark ef{gderint2}.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit coordinates: $\nabla(V)$ is cut out by $(\mathbb{D}(I))$ and $c_n$ acts on the coordinate tuple through the structural constants.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{D}'_V(a)$ lands in $\nabla V(L)$
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a $K$-scheme and suppose that $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(L,\mathbb{D}')$ is an extension of $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-fields. Then for any $a\in V(L)$, we have $\mathbb{D}'_V(a)\in\nabla V(L)$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a $K$-scheme and suppose that $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(L,\mathbb{D}')$ is an extension of $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-fields.
conclusions: for any $a\in V(L)$, we have $\mathbb{D}'_V(a)\in\nabla V(L)$

nodes.name: Proof that $\mathbb{D}'_V(a)\in\nabla V(L)$
nodes.statement: It is enough to notice that if $\mathbb{D}'$ extends $\mathbb{D}$, then the $k$-algebra map $\mathbb{D}':L\to \mathcal{D}(L)$ is $K$-linear.
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathbb{D}'$ extends $\mathbb{D}$ then $\mathbb{D}':L\to\mathcal{D}(L)$ is $K$-linear.

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity in terms of $\nabla$
nodes.statement: For any $K$-scheme $V$ we have the following: $$\mathbb{D}_{\nabla(V)}\circ \mathbb{D}_V=c_V\circ \mathbb{D}_V.$$
conclusions: $$\mathbb{D}_{\nabla(V)}\circ \mathbb{D}_V=c_V\circ \mathbb{D}_V.$$

nodes.name: The saturated field $\Omega$ and the loci $V,W$
nodes.statement: Let us fix a $|K|^+$-saturated algebraically closed field $\Omega$ containing $K$. We want to describe possible extensions of $\mathbb{D}$ to subfields of $\Omega$ in terms of the functor $\nabla$. Let $b_0\in\Omega^n$, $b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{p^{me}-1})\in\Omega^{np^{me}}$ and we set $$V=\locus_K(b_0),\ \ \ W=\locus_K(b).$$

nodes.name: Extending $\mathbb{D}$ to $K(b)$
nodes.statement: If $b\in \nabla V(\Omega)$ and $K(b_0)=K(b)$, then there is an $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $K(b)$ extending $\mathbb{D}$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$.
conclusions: there is an $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $K(b)$ extending $\mathbb{D}$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$

nodes.name: Criterion $c_n(W)\subseteq\nabla(W)$ for extending the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation
nodes.statement: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There is a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$. \item There is a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(L,\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$. \item $c_{n}(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension realizing $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$ exists iff $c_n(W)\subseteq\nabla(W)$.
conclusions: There is a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$.
There is a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq(L,\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$.
$c_{n}(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$.

nodes.name: Geometric axioms for $\gdcf$
nodes.statement: {\bf Geometric axioms for $\gdcf$} \begin{enumerate} \item The field $K$ is separably closed. \item For each positive integer $n$, suppose that $V\subseteq {\mathbb A}^n$ and $W\subseteq \nabla(V)$ are absolutely irreducible $K$-varieties, and $Z$ is a proper $K$-subvariety of $W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$, and $c_{V}(W)\subseteq \nabla (W)$, then there is $a\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}_{V}(a)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: $K$ is separably closed, and every $W\subseteq\nabla(V)$ projecting generically onto $V$ with $c_V(W)\subseteq\nabla(W)$ has a $K$-point of $\mathbb{D}_V$ off any proper subvariety $Z$.

nodes.name: The geometric axioms are first-order
nodes.statement: These axioms are first-order, since for a separably closed field $K$, any $K$-irreducible variety is absolutely irreducible.
conclusions: These axioms are first-order

nodes.name: Geometric axiomatization of existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-fields
nodes.statement: The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field if and only if $(K,\mathbb{D})$ satisfies the geometric axioms above.
conclusions: The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field if and only if $(K,\mathbb{D})$ satisfies the geometric axioms above.

nodes.name: Proof of the geometric axiomatization
nodes.statement:
Assume that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field. Then by Proposition ef{etalegext}, $K$ is separably closed (since a separable algebraic field extension is '{e}tale). Take any $K$-irreducible $K$-varieties $V\subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$, $W\subseteq 
abla(V)$ and $Z\subsetneq W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$ then there is $b_0\in\Omega^n$ and $b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{p^{me}-1})\in\Omega^{np^{me}}$ such that $V=\locus_K(b_0)$ and $W=\locus_K(b)$. Since $c_V(W)\subseteq 
abla(W)$, Lemma ef{cVW} implies that there exists a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$. We have $$\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b\in W(K(b))\setminus Z(K(b))$$ and $b_0\in V(K(b))$. Since $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is existentially closed, there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}_V(b'_0)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$. \ \ Assume now that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is a model of the ``geometric axioms for $\gdcf$'' and let $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (L,\mathbb{D}')$ be an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields. Take any quantifier-free formula $\varphi(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^{me}-1})$ over $K$ (in the language of fields), where each $x_i$ is an $n$-tuple of variables for an arbitrary (but fixed) positive integer $n$. Suppose that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(x_0))$. Take $b_0\in L^n$ such that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(b_0))$ and set $$V=\locus_K(b_0),\ \ b=\mathbb{D}_V'(b_0),\ \ W=\locus_K(b),\ \ Z_0=\lbrace d\in W\;\;|\;\; 
eg\varphi(d)brace.$$ Let $Z$ denote the intersection of all $K$-subvarieties of $W$ containing $Z_0$. Clearly $b\in W(L)\setminus Z(L)$ and the second condition of Lemma ef{cVW} is satisfied, so $c_{V}(W)\subseteq 
abla(W)$. Hence all the assumptions of the ``geometric axioms for $\gdcf$'' hold. Therefore there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}(b_0')\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$ and $(K,\mathbb{D})\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}(x_0))$.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions translate a witness between $K$ and an extension using the criterion $c_V(W)\subseteq\nabla(W)$.

nodes.name: Forward direction: separable closedness
nodes.statement: Assume that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field. Then by Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $K$ is separably closed (since a separable algebraic field extension is \'{e}tale).
nodes.statement_short: An existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field is separably closed since separable algebraic extensions are étale.

nodes.name: Realize the configuration in an extension
nodes.statement: Take any $K$-irreducible $K$-varieties $V\subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$, $W\subseteq \nabla(V)$ and $Z\subsetneq W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$ then there is $b_0\in\Omega^n$ and $b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{p^{me}-1})\in\Omega^{np^{me}}$ such that $V=\locus_K(b_0)$ and $W=\locus_K(b)$. Since $c_V(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$, Lemma \ref{cVW} implies that there exists a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$. We have $$\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b\in W(K(b))\setminus Z(K(b))$$ and $b_0\in V(K(b))$.
nodes.statement_short: The criterion produces a $\mathfrak{g}$-extension $K(b)$ with $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$.

nodes.name: Pull the point back to $K$
nodes.statement: Since $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is existentially closed, there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}_V(b'_0)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$. \\ \\
nodes.statement_short: Existential closedness gives $b_0'\in V(K)$ with $\mathbb{D}_V(b_0')\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$.

nodes.name: Converse: set up loci from a witness
nodes.statement: Assume now that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is a model of the ``geometric axioms for $\gdcf$'' and let $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (L,\mathbb{D}')$ be an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields. Take any quantifier-free formula $\varphi(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^{me}-1})$ over $K$ (in the language of fields), where each $x_i$ is an $n$-tuple of variables for an arbitrary (but fixed) positive integer $n$. Suppose that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(x_0))$. Take $b_0\in L^n$ such that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(b_0))$ and set $$V=\locus_K(b_0),\ \ b=\mathbb{D}_V'(b_0),\ \ W=\locus_K(b),\ \ Z_0=\lbrace d\in W\;\;|\;\; \neg\varphi(d)\rbrace.$$
nodes.statement_short: From a witness in an extension $L$ build $V$, $b$, $W$ and the bad locus $Z_0$.

nodes.name: Apply the axioms to find a witness in $K$
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ denote the intersection of all $K$-subvarieties of $W$ containing $Z_0$. Clearly $b\in W(L)\setminus Z(L)$ and the second condition of Lemma \ref{cVW} is satisfied, so $c_{V}(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$. Hence all the assumptions of the ``geometric axioms for $\gdcf$'' hold. Therefore there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}(b_0')\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$ and $(K,\mathbb{D})\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}(x_0))$.
nodes.statement_short: The axioms give $b_0'\in V(K)$ realizing the same quantifier-free formula.

nodes.name: The axiomatization does not use Section 4
nodes.statement: Note that the results of Section \ref{secmc} are not used in the proof of Theorem \ref{ggeo} which suggests a possibility of generalizations, e.g. to the context of $\mathcal{D}$-fields from \cite{MS}.

nodes.name: Geometric axioms for $\fdcf$
nodes.statement: {\bf Geometric axioms for $\fdcf$} \begin{enumerate} \item The field $K$ is separably closed. \item For any positive integers $n,m$, suppose that $V\subseteq {\mathbb A}^n$ and $W\subseteq \nabla_m(V)$ are absolutely irreducible $K$-varieties, and $Z$ is a proper $K$-subvariety of $W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$, and $c_{m,V}(W)\subseteq \nabla_m(W)$, then there is $a\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}[m]_{V}(a)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: The truncated axioms, taken for all $m$ simultaneously with $\nabla_m$ and $c_{m,V}$.

nodes.name: Geometric axiomatization of existentially closed $F$-fields
nodes.statement: The $F$-field $\mathbf{K}$ is an existentially closed $F$-field if and only if $\mathbf{K}$ is a model of the geometric axioms for $\gdcf$.
conclusions: The $F$-field $\mathbf{K}$ is an existentially closed $F$-field if and only if $\mathbf{K}$ is a model of the geometric axioms for $\gdcf$.

nodes.name: Section 4 is needed for the untruncated axiomatization
nodes.statement: Unlike in the proof of Theorem \ref{ggeo}, the results of Section \ref{secmc} \emph{are} used for the proof of Theorem \ref{fgeo}, since Theorem \ref{chain} is necessary for the geometric axiomatization and the proof of Theorem \ref{chain} requires the algebraic axiomatizations of $\gdcf$ and $\fdcf$. However, one can also prove Theorem \ref{chain} (but for a limited class of formal groups $F$ only) in another fashion as it was done in \cite{K3} for $F=\widehat{\ga^e}$. This approach will be discussed in Section \ref{secgtup}.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the truncated case, the $F$-version needs the chain theorem and hence the algebraic axiomatizations.

nodes.name: Extending the techniques to iterative $\underline{\mathcal{D}}$-fields
nodes.statement: One could wonder whether our techniques may be generalized to include the case of iterative $\underline{\mathcal{D}}$-fields of positive characteristic. It seems likely in the case where an iterative system $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$ is the inverse limit of finite iterative systems $(\mathcal{D}_m,\Delta_m)_m$ resembling the ones given by Hopf algebra comultiplications $\mu_m:\mathcal{D}_m\to \mathcal{D}_m\circ \mathcal{D}_m$ (see Section \ref{secproco}). More precisely, our techniques may apply to the iterative systems $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$ where each morphism $\Delta_{p^m}:\mathcal{D}_{2p^m}\to \mathcal{D}_{p^m}\circ \mathcal{D}_{p^m}$ factors through the projection morphism $\mathcal{D}_{2p^m}\to \mathcal{D}_{p^m}$. It is easy to see that each direct system of finite group schemes provides such an iterative system, and, for example, \'{e}tale group schemes (corresponding to actual groups) would correspond to systems governing actions of groups on fields by field automorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Do the methods extend to iterative $\underline{\mathcal{D}}$-fields of positive characteristic, e.g. inverse limits of Hopf-comultiplication systems?

nodes.name: canonical $G$-tuple
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be a $G[m]$-derivation on $K$. A subset $B\subseteq K$ is called a \emph{canonical $G$-tuple}, if $|B|=e$ and there is a $G[m]$-embedding $(k(G),\mathbb{D}[m]^G)\to \mathbf{K}$ such that $B$ is the image of the set of canonical parameters of $G$, where $\mathbb{D}[m]^G$ is the canonical $G[m]$-derivation from Example \ref{cangex}.
nodes.statement_short: An $e$-element subset of $K$ that is the image of the canonical parameters of $G$ under a $G[m]$-embedding of $(k(G),\mathbb{D}[m]^G)$.
differentia: if $|B|=e$ and there is a $G[m]$-embedding $(k(G),\mathbb{D}[m]^G)\to \mathbf{K}$ such that $B$ is the image of the set of canonical parameters of $G$

nodes.name: Canonical $G$-tuples are $p$-bases
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and of imperfection degree $e$, then any canonical $G$-tuple in $L$ is a $p$-basis. For $G=\ga^e$, we recover the notion of a \emph{canonical $p$-basis} from \cite{Zieg2}.
nodes.statement_short: In a strict $L$ of imperfection degree $e$ any canonical $G$-tuple is a $p$-basis, recovering Ziegler's canonical $p$-basis for $G=\ga^e$.

nodes.name: existence of canonical $G$-tuples
nodes.statement: We say that \emph{canonical $G$-tuples exist} if for any $m$ and any separably closed $G[m]$-field $\mathbf{L}$, whenever $[L:C_L]=p^e$, there is a canonical $G$-tuple in $L$.

nodes.name: Generalizations and known cases for canonical $G$-tuples
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Definition \ref{defpbasis} can be phrased in a (much) greater generality using group scheme actions. Let $\mathfrak{G}_0$ be a group subscheme of a group scheme $\mathfrak{G}$. Assume that $\mathfrak{G}_0$ acts (as a group scheme) on a scheme $V$. We say that this action has a \emph{canonical $\mathfrak{G}$-basis}, if there is an $\mathfrak{G}_0$-invariant morphism $V\to \mathfrak{G}$ such that the induced map $$V\to \mathfrak{G}\times_{\mathfrak{G}/\mathfrak{G}_0}V/\mathfrak{G}_0$$ is an isomorphism. \item The existence of canonical $\mathbb{G}_a^e$-tuples is shown in \cite{Zieg2} and the existence of canonical $\mathbb{G}_m$-tuples is shown in \cite{HK1}. Combining these results, one can show the existence of canonical $G$-tuples for $G$ of the form $\mathbb{G}_a^e\times\mathbb{G}_m^f$. \item We do not attack here the problem of the \emph{existence} of canonical $G$-tuples for a given algebraic group $G$. This will be done in \cite{Hoff1} (as well as possible applications to the notion of ``$G$-thinness''). \item The existence of canonical $G$-tuples implies (\emph{strong}) \emph{integrability} of $G$-derivations, as in (morally) \cite{Mats1} or as in \cite{HK1} (see also \cite{Tyc}) \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The notion generalizes to group scheme actions; existence is known for $\ga^e$, $\gm$ and their products, and implies integrability.

nodes.name: Existence of canonical $G$-tuples for a given algebraic group $G$
nodes.statement: We do not attack here the problem of the \emph{existence} of canonical $G$-tuples for a given algebraic group $G$. This will be done in \cite{Hoff1} (as well as possible applications to the notion of ``$G$-thinness'').

nodes.name: Canonical $G$-tuples yield another proof of the chain theorem
nodes.statement: The existence of canonical $G$-tuples gives rather directly (see \cite[Thm. 2.3]{K3}) another proof of Theorem \ref{chain} which is the only ingredient needed in Section \ref{secaxioms} requiring specific differential-algebraic arguments.
conclusions: another proof of Theorem \ref{chain} which is the only ingredient needed in Section \ref{secaxioms} requiring specific differential-algebraic arguments
